<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:conductor-different}
Let $\mathfrak{C}_\theta$ denote the conductor of the order
$\mathbb Z[\theta]$ in $\mathcal O_K$, and let
$\mathfrak D_K=\mathfrak D_{\mathcal O_K/\mathbb Z}$ be the different of
$K$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cd}
\mathfrak{C}_\theta\,\mathfrak D_K=(f'(\theta)).
\end{equation}
In particular,
$f'(\theta)\in\mathfrak{C}_\theta .$
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:different}
Let $\mathfrak m$ be a prime ideal of $\mathcal O_K$ lying above a
prime $p$, and suppose that
$p\mathcal O_K=\mathfrak m^{\,e}\mathfrak a,~\mathfrak m\nmid\mathfrak a.$
Then
$\mathfrak m^{\,e-1}\mid\mathfrak D_K.$
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:pmax}
The order $\mathbb Z[\theta]$ is $p$-maximal if and only if $\mathfrak{C}_\theta+p\mathcal O_K=\mathcal O_K.$
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Let $G=\mathcal O_K/\mathbb Z[\theta]$ be a finite abelian group, and let
$N=|G|$.

Firstly, suppose that
\(
\mathfrak{C}_\theta+p\mathcal O_K=\mathcal O_K.
\)
So, there exist $c\in\mathfrak{C}_\theta$ and $u\in\mathcal O_K$ such that
$1=c+pu$. For every $x\in\mathcal O_K$, we have $x=cx+pux,$
where $cx\in\mathbb Z[\theta]$. Hence,
$\mathcal O_K=\mathbb Z[\theta]+p\mathcal O_K,$
and hence $G=pG$. Since $G$ is finite, its $p$-primary component is trivial, and
therefore $p\nmid N$.

Now, suppose that $p\nmid N$. Since $NG=0$, we have
$N\mathcal O_K\subseteq\mathbb Z[\theta],$
so $N\in\mathfrak{C}_\theta$. By B\'ezout's identity, there exist
$a,b\in\mathbb Z$ such that
$aN+bp=1.$
Hence
$1\in\mathfrak{C}_\theta+p\mathcal O_K,$
which completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:intmem}
Let $\mathfrak m$ be a maximal ideal of $\mathcal O_K$ lying above a prime $p$. Then, for every $t\in\mathbb Z$,
\[
t\in\mathfrak m
\iff
p\mid t.
\]
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Since $\mathfrak m\cap\mathbb Z$
is a non-zero prime ideal of $\mathbb Z$ containing $p$, it follows that
$\mathfrak m\cap\mathbb Z=p\mathbb Z,$
which proves the claim.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:eis}
If the minimal polynomial $f$ of $\theta$ is Eisenstein at a prime $p$, then
$\mathbb Z[\theta]$ is $p$-maximal.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:suff}
Let $f\in\mathbb Z[X]$ be a monic irreducible polynomial, and let
$\theta$ be a root of $f$. Let $r \in \mathbb{Z}$ satisfy
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $p^2 \nmid f(r)$;
\item[(ii)] $p \nmid f''(r)$;
\item[(iii)] every maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ of $\mathcal{O}_K$ with $\mathfrak{C}_\theta \subseteq \mathfrak{m}$ and $p \in \mathfrak{m}$
contains $\theta - r$.
\end{enumerate}
Then $\mathbb{Z}[\theta]$ is $p$-maximal.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Suppose that $\mathbb{Z}[\theta]$ is not $p$-maximal. By Lemma~\ref{lem:pmax},
\[
\mathfrak{C}_\theta+p\,\mathcal{O}_K\neq\mathcal{O}_K,
\]
so there exists a maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ of $\mathcal{O}_K$ containing
$\mathfrak{C}_\theta+p\,\mathcal{O}_K$. By hypothesis~$\it{(iii)}$,
$\pi:=\theta-r\in\mathfrak{m}.$

Consider the first-order Taylor expansion of $f'$ at $r$, i.e.,
\begin{equation*}\label{eq:taylor1}
f'=f'(r)+(X-r)g_1,\qquad g_1(r)=f''(r),
\end{equation*}
and set
$S=g(\theta),~ T=g_1(\theta).$
Then \eqref{eq:fund} holds and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fprime}
f'(\theta)=f'(r)+\pi T.
\end{equation}

Since $f'(\theta)\in\mathfrak{C}_\theta\subseteq\mathfrak{m}$ and $\pi\in\mathfrak{m}$,
identity~\eqref{eq:fprime} implies that $f'(r)\in\mathfrak{m}$. Hence
$p\mid f'(r)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:intmem}. Equation~\eqref{eq:fund}
then shows that $f(r)\in\mathfrak{m}$, and therefore $p\mid f(r)$. Write
$f(r)=pt,\text{ where }p\nmid t, \text{ and }
f'(r)=pk.$



We next show that $S,T\notin\mathfrak{m}$. Indeed, for every
$q\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$, we have 
$q(\theta)-q(r)\in(\theta-r)\subseteq\mathfrak{m}.$
Thus $q(\theta)\in\mathfrak{m}$ would imply $q(r)\in\mathfrak{m}$, or equivalently,
$p\mid q(r)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:intmem}. Since
\[
g_1(r)=f''(r),\qquad 2g(r)=f''(r),
\]
hypothesis~{\it{(ii)}} yields
\[
p\nmid g(r)\qquad\text{and}\qquad p\nmid g_1(r),
\]
and consequently
$S,T\notin\mathfrak{m}.$ Now set
$\sigma=t+k\pi.$
Then \eqref{eq:fund} becomes
\begin{equation}\label{eq:idideal}
\pi^2S=-p\sigma,
\qquad\text{or equivalently}\qquad
(\pi)^2(S)=(p)(\sigma)
\end{equation}
as ideals of $\mathcal{O}_K$. Furthermore, $\sigma\notin\mathfrak{m}$.                                                                         
Also,
$\pi\neq0$ because $\deg f\ge2$. Let
\[
w=v_{\mathfrak{m}}((\pi)),\qquad
e=v_{\mathfrak{m}}((p)).
\] Since
$v_{\mathfrak{m}}((S))=v_{\mathfrak{m}}((\sigma))=0$, taking $\mathfrak{m}$-adic valuations
in~\eqref{eq:idideal}, we have  $2w=e.$ We claim that
$f'(\theta)\notin\mathfrak{m}^{\,w+1}.$
By~\eqref{eq:fprime},
$\pi T=f'(\theta)-pk.$
Since
$p\in\mathfrak{m}^{\,e}
=\mathfrak{m}^{2w}
\subseteq\mathfrak{m}^{\,w+1},$
the assumption $f'(\theta)\in\mathfrak{m}^{\,w+1}$ would imply
$\pi T\in\mathfrak{m}^{\,w+1}$. On the other hand,
$v_{\mathfrak{m}}((\pi T))
=v_{\mathfrak{m}}((\pi))+v_{\mathfrak{m}}((T))
=w,$
because $T\notin\mathfrak{m}$. This contradicts
$\pi T\in\mathfrak{m}^{\,w+1}$.

Finally, since $\mathfrak{m}^{\,e}\mid p\,\mathcal{O}_K,$
Proposition~\ref{prop:different} gives
$\mathfrak{m}^{\,e-1}\mid\mathfrak{d}_K.$
Moreover,
$\mathfrak{m}\mid\mathfrak{C}_\theta$
by construction. Hence, using the conductor--different
identity~\eqref{eq:cd},
\[
\mathfrak{m}^{\,e}
=\mathfrak{m}^{\,1+(e-1)}
\mid
\mathfrak{C}_\theta\mathfrak{d}_K
=(f'(\theta)).
\]
Therefore
$f'(\theta)\in\mathfrak{m}^{\,e}
=\mathfrak{m}^{2w}
\subseteq\mathfrak{m}^{\,w+1},$
which is a contradiction. Thus $\mathbb{Z}[\theta]$ is $p$-maximal.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:nec}
Let $f\in\mathbb Z[X]$ be a monic irreducible polynomial, and let
$\theta$ be a root of $f$. 
Suppose $p^2 \mid f(r)$ and $p \mid f'(r)$. Then $p \mid I[\theta]$; in particular
$\mathbb{Z}[\theta] \ne \mathcal{O}_K$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Write $f(r) = p^2 t,~f'(r) = pk$, and set
$y =\pi S = (\theta - r)\,~g(\theta) \ \in\ \mathbb{Z}[\theta].$
Multiplying~\eqref{eq:fund} by $S$, we have $y^2 = -f(r)S - f'(r)y$, i.e.
\begin{equation*}\label{eq:quad}
  y^2 + f'(r)\,y + f(r)\,S = 0,
  \qquad\text{ and hence}\qquad
  \Bigl(\frac{y}{p}\Bigr)^{\!2} + k\Bigl(\frac{y}{p}\Bigr) + t\,S \ =\ 0.
\end{equation*}
Thus $z := y/p \in K$ satisfies a {monic} quadratic polynomial over $\mathcal{O}_K$, so $z \in \mathcal{O}_K$.

We claim $z \notin \mathbb{Z}[\theta]$. Suppose $z = c(\theta)$ for some $c \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$; without loss of generality, we may assume $\deg c < n$. Consider
$ W \ =\ (X - r)\,g \ \in\ \mathbb{Z}[X],$
which by~\eqref{eq:taylor2} is a monic polynomial of degree $n-1$, and satisfies $W(\theta) = y = p\,c(\theta)$.
Then $W - p\,c$ vanishes at $\theta$ and has degree $< n = \deg f$, so $W = p\,c$ identically.
Comparing leading coefficients, we get a contradiction. Thus $z \notin \mathbb Z[\theta]$ but $pz\in\mathbb Z[\theta]$. Therefore the class of $z$ in $\mathcal O_K/\mathbb Z[\theta]$ has order $p$, and hence, the proof is complete.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The search of a suitable integer \(r\) satisfying the hypotheses of  Theorem~\ref{thm:nec} can  be restricted to values of $r$ such that $0\le r<p^2$  as both $f(r)\bmod p^2$ and $f'(r)\bmod p$ depend only on
$r\bmod p^2$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
The converse of Theorem~\ref{thm:nec} is not true. 
For example, consider $
f(X)=X^4+2X^3+5X^2+4X+7.
$ Here $f$ does not satisfy the hypotheses of Theorem 3.2, but it is non-monogenic.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thmm:necfactor}
Let $f\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$ be monic irreducible polynomial of degree $n$ with a root $\theta$, and let $p$ be a
prime. Let $\bar\varphi$ be a repeated irreducible factor of $\bar f$ in
$\mathbb{F}_p[X]$ of degree $d$, let $\varphi\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$ be a monic lift of $\bar{\varphi}$, and  $\alpha$ be a root of
$\varphi$. Suppose that $f=\sum_k a_k\varphi^{\,k}$  where $\deg a_k<d$  is the $\varphi$-adic expansion of $f$.
 If
$p^2\mid a_0 ,$ then $p\mid I(\theta)$; in particular $f$ is non-monogenic.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
It is easy to check that  $p\mid a_1$ and $p\mid f'(\alpha)$. 
Write $a_0=p^2t$, $a_1=pk$ with $t,k\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$, and $G=\sum_{k\ge2}a_k\varphi^{\,k-2}$. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:obstruction}
f=\varphi^2G+p\,k\varphi+p^2t .
\end{equation}
Set $W=\varphi G$, which is monic of degree $n-d$, and
\[
y=W(\theta)=\varphi(\theta)G(\theta)\in\mathbb{Z}[\theta],
\qquad
z=\frac{y}{p}\in K=\mathbb{Q}(\theta).
\]
We show that $z\in\mathcal{O}_K\setminus\mathbb{Z}[\theta]$. Since $pz=y\in\mathbb{Z}[\theta]$, the
class of $z$ is an element of order $p$ of the finite group
$\mathcal{O}_K/\mathbb{Z}[\theta]$, and thus $p\mid I(\theta)$. Evaluating \eqref{eq:obstruction} at
$\theta$ and using $f(\theta)=0$, we have
$\varphi(\theta)^2G(\theta)=-p\bigl(k(\theta)\varphi(\theta)+p\,t(\theta)\bigr)$.
Multiplying by $G(\theta)$, and then dividing by $p^2$, we get
$z^2+k(\theta)\,z+t(\theta)G(\theta)=0 .$
Thus $z\in\mathcal{O}_K$.


It remains to prove that $z\not\in \mathbb{Z}[\theta]$. The set $\{1,\theta,\dots,\theta^{\,n-1}\}$ form
a $\mathbb{Z}$-basis of $\mathbb{Z}[\theta]$, and $\deg W<n$, so the coefficients of $W$
are the coordinates of $y$ in that basis.  If $z=y/p\in \mathbb{Z}[\theta]$,
all of them would be divisible by $p$. So $z\not\in \mathbb{Z}[\theta]$ because $W$ is monic.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{th1}
Let $A,B\in\mathbb{Z}$ with $B\neq0$, and let $n,m$ be positive integers satisfying $1\le m<n,~ n>2.$
Assume that $\gcd(n,mB)=1$. Let
$f(X)=X^n+A(BX+1)^m$
be irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$, and let $D=n^n+(-1)^{n+m}B^n(n-m)^{\,n-m}m^mA.$
Then $f$ is monogenic, if and only if both $A$ and $D$ are square-free.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor}
	Let $p$ be a prime number, $n, m$ and  $B$ be positive integers with $1\le m\le n-1,~n>2$ and $\gcd(n,mB)=1.$ Then $f(X)=X^n+p(BX+1)^m$ is monogenic if and only if   $n^n+(-1)^{n+m}B^n(n-m)^{n-m}m^mp$ is square-free.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:cong}
Let $f,~D$ be as above and $a, N \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $N \mid B(n-m)a + n$. Then
\[
  \bigl(B(n-m)\bigr)^n f(a) \ \equiv\ (-1)^n D \pmod N.
\]
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Set $z = B(n-m)$, so that $za \equiv -n \pmod N$. Note that,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:aux}
  (n-m)(Ba+1) \ =\ za + (n-m) \ \equiv\ -n + (n-m) \ =\ -m \pmod N.
\end{equation}
So, keeping in mind \eqref{eq:fa}, we have
\begin{align*}
  z^n f(a)
  &= (za)^n + A\,B^n (n-m)^n (Ba+1)^m\\
  &= (za)^n + A\,B^n (n-m)^{n-m}\bigl((n-m)(Ba+1)\bigr)^m\\
  &\equiv (-n)^n + A\,B^n (n-m)^{n-m}(-m)^m \pmod N\\
  &= (-1)^n\Bigl(n^n + (-1)^{n+m} B^n (n-m)^{n-m} m^m A\Bigr) \ =\ (-1)^n D. \qedhere
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:cong}
If $\gcd\bigl(N,\ B(n-m)\bigr) = 1$, then $N \mid f(a)$ if and only if $N \mid D$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:bezout}
If $p \nmid B(n-m)$, there exists $a \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $p^2 \mid B(n-m)\,a + n$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Since $p\nmid B(n-m)$, the congruence $B(n-m)a\equiv-n\pmod{p^2}$ has a solution.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:coprime}
Let $f,~D$ be as above and assume  that $\gcd(n,\ mB) = 1$. If $p \nmid A$ and $p \mid D$, then $p \nmid n$, $p \nmid B$,
$p \nmid m$, and $p \nmid n-m$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
First suppose that $p \mid n$. Since $\gcd(n,mB)=1$, we have
$p \nmid m$ and $p \nmid B$. 
As $p\mid D$ and $p\mid n^n$, it follows that
$p\mid B^n(n-m)^{\,n-m}m^mA.$
Hence $p$ divides one of $B$, $n-m$, $m$, or $A$. The first, third, and fourth
possibilities contradict $p\nmid B$, $p\nmid m$, and $p\nmid A$, respectively.
If $p\mid n-m$, then together with the fact that $p\mid n$, we obtain that $p\mid m$, again a
contradiction. Therefore $p\nmid n$.

Now suppose that $p$ divides one of $B$, $m$, or $n-m$. Since $p\nmid n$, we
have $p\nmid n^n$. On the other hand,
$D-n^n=(-1)^{n+m}B^n(n-m)^{\,n-m}m^mA$
is divisible by $p$, and hence so is $D-n^n$. As $p\mid D$, this implies
$p\mid n^n$, contradicting $p\nmid n$. Thus
$p\nmid B$, $p\nmid m$, and $p\nmid n-m$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:sqA}
Assume $ \gcd(n,\ mB) = 1$. If $p \mid A$ and $p^2 \mid D$, then $p^2 \mid A$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
From $p \mid A$ and $p \mid D$, we get $p \mid n^n$, hence $p \mid n$; then the hypothesis
gives $p \nmid m, B$, and consequently $p \nmid n-m$. Since $n \ge 2$ we get $p^2 \mid n^n$, so
$p^2$ divides $D - n^n = (-1)^{n+m}B^n (n-m)^{n-m} m^m A$, all of whose factors except $A$ are
coprime to $p$. Hence $p^2 \mid A$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:residue}
Assume that \eqref{eq:str} holds. Let $x \in F$ be a common root of $\bar f$ and $\bar f'$. Then $x \ne 0$, $u \ne 0$,
$p \nmid n$, $p \nmid B$, $p \nmid m$, $p \nmid n-m$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:lin}
  (\bar n - \bar m)\,\bar B\,x \ =\ -\,\bar n.
\end{equation}
In particular; the coefficient $(\bar n - \bar m)\bar B$ is invertible, so $x$ is uniquely
determined by~\eqref{eq:lin} and lies in the prime field of $F$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Since $\bar f(x)=0$, we have $x\neq0$, for otherwise
$\bar f(x)=\bar A\neq0$. Similarly, $u\neq0$, since otherwise
$\bar f(x)=x^n\neq0$. Combining \eqref{eq:fa} and \eqref{eq:fpa}, we obtain
\begin{align}
0
&=\bar n\,\bar f(x)-x\,\bar f'(x)\notag\\
&=\bar n\bigl(x^n+\bar Au^m\bigr)
-x\bigl(\bar n x^{n-1}+\bar m\bar A\bar Bu^{m-1}\bigr)\notag\\
&=\bar A u^{m-1}\bigl(\bar nu-\bar m\bar Bx\bigr).
\label{eq:collapse}
\end{align}
Since $\bar A\neq0$ and $u\neq0$, it follows that
$\bar nu=\bar m\bar Bx$, which is equivalent to
\eqref{eq:lin}.

We next prove that $p\nmid n$, $p\nmid B$, $p\nmid m$, and
$p\nmid(n-m)$. If $p\mid n$, then $\bar n=0$. Since $p\nmid A$ and
$\gcd(n,mB)=1$, we have $\bar A,\bar B,\bar m\neq0$.
Hence $\bar f'(x)=\bar m\bar A\bar Bu^{m-1}\neq0,$
contradicting $\bar f'(x)=0$. Thus $p\nmid n$.
If $p\mid B$, then \eqref{eq:lin} gives $0=-\bar n$, contradicting
$p\nmid n$. The case $p\mid(n-m)$ is identical. Finally, if
$p\mid m$, then $\bar m=0$, so \eqref{eq:lin} yields
$\bar Bx=-1$, that is, $u=0$, again a contradiction. Hence $(\bar n-\bar m)\bar B$ is invertible. Therefore
\eqref{eq:lin} uniquely determines $x$, and consequently
$x$ belongs to the prime field of $F$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:Dzero}
Assume that \eqref{eq:str} holds. Let $x\in F$ satisfy
\eqref{eq:lin}, and suppose that
$p\nmid nBm(n-m).$
Then
$\bar f(x)=\bar f'(x)=0
~\Longleftrightarrow~
\bar D=0
\ \text{in }F.$
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
By \eqref{eq:lin}, $(\bar n-\bar m)u=-\bar m.$
Raising 
$(\bar n-\bar m)\bar Bx=-\bar n
~\text{and}~
(\bar n-\bar m)u=-\bar m$
to the powers $n$ and $m$, respectively, and arguing exactly as in the proof
of Lemma~\ref{lem:cong}, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fieldcong}
\bigl((\bar n-\bar m)\bar B\bigr)^n\bar f(x)
=
(-1)^n\bar D.
\end{equation}
Since $(\bar n-\bar m)\bar B$ is invertible, it follows that
$\bar f(x)=0
~\Longleftrightarrow~
\bar D=0.$ It remains to prove that $\bar f(x)=0
~\Longrightarrow~
\bar f'(x)=0.$
From \eqref{eq:lin}, we have $x\neq0$, for otherwise $\bar n=0$.
Moreover, $(\bar n-\bar m)u=-\bar m$
shows that $u\neq0$, since $p\nmid m$ and $p\nmid(n-m)$. Multiplying
$\bar f'(x)$ by the nonzero element $xu$ and using
$\bar n u=\bar m\bar Bx$, we obtain
$\bar f'(x)\,xu
=
\bar nux^n+\bar m\bar A\bar Bxu^m
=
\bar nu\bigl(x^n+\bar Au^m\bigr)
=
\bar nu\,\bar f(x)
=
0.$
Hence $\bar f'(x)=0$, which completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:tame}
Assume that \eqref{eq:str} holds. Let $x\in F$ satisfy $\bar f(x)=\bar f'(x)=0.$
Then $\bar f''(x)\neq0.$
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Since $\bar f(x)=\bar f'(x)=0$, Proposition~\ref{prop:residue}
shows that \eqref{eq:lin} holds. As
$u=\bar Bx+1,$
equation~\eqref{eq:lin} yields
$(\bar n-\bar m)\bar Bx=-\bar n,$
from which we obtain
$-(\bar n-1)u+(\bar m-1)\bar Bx=1.$ Multiplying \eqref{eq:fppa} by the nonzero element $xu$ and using
$\bar f'(x)=0$, we obtain $\bar f''(x)\,xu
=
\bar m\,\bar A\,\bar B\,u^{m-1}.$
Since $\bar A$, $\bar B$, $\bar m$, and $u$ are nonzero, the right-hand side
does not vanish. As $xu\neq0$, we conclude that
$\bar f''(x)\neq0.$
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Let $\theta$ be a root of $f(X)=X^n+A(BX+1)^m,$
and  $K=\mathbb{Q}(\theta)$. Let $p$ be a prime. Note that $f(0)=A
~\text{and}~
f'(0)=mAB.$
                                                                                


First, suppose that $p^2\mid A$. Since $p^2\mid f(0)
\quad\text{and}\quad
p\mid f'(0),$
Theorem~\ref{thm:nec} yields $p\mid I[\theta].$

Next assume that $p^2\mid D$ and $p\mid A$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:sqA},
we have $p^2\mid A$, so the previous case applies.

Finally, assume that $p^2\mid D$ and $p\nmid A$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:coprime}, we have $p\nmid B(n-m)$. Let $a$ be as in
Lemma~\ref{lem:bezout}, so that $p^2\mid B(n-m)a+n.$
Applying Corollary~\ref{cor:cong} with $N=p^2$, we obtain
\[
p^2\mid f(a)
\iff
p^2\mid D.
\]
Hence $p^2\mid f(a)$. Moreover, the residue class $\bar a$ satisfies
\eqref{eq:lin} over $\mathbb{F}_p$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:Dzero},
$\bar f'(\bar a)=0,$
and therefore $p\mid f'(a).$
Applying Theorem~\ref{thm:nec} with $r=a$, we conclude that
$p\mid I[\theta].$

For the converse, we prove it by contraposition. Assume that
$p^2\nmid A
\quad\text{and}\quad
p^2\nmid D.$
We shall prove that $\mathbb{Z}[\theta]$ is $p$-maximal.

Suppose first that $p\mid A$. Since $p^2\nmid A$, every coefficient of
$f$ except the leading one is divisible by $p$, while the constant term
$A$ is not divisible by $p^2$. Hence $f$ is Eisenstein at $p$, and the
result follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:eis}.

Now assume that $p\nmid A$ and $p\mid D$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:coprime}, $p\nmid n B m(n-m).$
Let $a$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:bezout}, so that
$p^2\mid B(n-m)a+n.$ By Corollary~\ref{cor:cong},  
$p^2\nmid f(a),$
since $p^2\nmid D$. The residue class $\bar a$ satisfies
\eqref{eq:lin}. Since $p\mid D$, Proposition~\ref{prop:Dzero} implies
that
$\bar f(\bar a)=\bar f'(\bar a)=0.$
Hence Proposition~\ref{prop:tame} gives
$\bar f''(\bar a)\neq0,$
and therefore $p\nmid f''(a).$ Let $\mathfrak{m}$ be a maximal ideal satisfying
$\mathfrak{C}_\theta\subseteq\mathfrak{m}
\quad\text{and}\quad
p\in\mathfrak{m},$
and put $F=\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{m}$. Reducing modulo $\mathfrak{m}$, we obtain $\bar f(\bar\theta)=0.$
Moreover,
$f'(\theta)\in\mathfrak{C}_\theta\subseteq\mathfrak{m}$
by the conductor-different identity~\eqref{eq:cd}, so
$\bar f'(\bar\theta)=0.$
Proposition~\ref{prop:residue} therefore shows that $\bar\theta$
satisfies~\eqref{eq:lin}. On the other hand, $p\mid B(n-m)a+n,$
so $\bar a$ also satisfies~\eqref{eq:lin} in $\mathbb{F}_p$. Since
$(\bar n-\bar m)\bar B$ is invertible in $\mathbb{F}_p$, the solution of
\eqref{eq:lin} is unique. Consequently,
$\bar\theta=\bar a
\quad\text{in }\mathbb{F}_p,$
or equivalently,
$\theta-a\in\mathfrak{m}.$ Hence, all the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:suff} are therefore satisfied,
and hence $\mathbb{Z}[\theta]$ is $p$-maximal.

Finally, assume that $p\nmid A$ and $p\nmid D$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:pmax}, it is enough to prove that no maximal ideal
contains $\mathfrak{C}_\theta+p\mathcal{O}_K$. Suppose, to the contrary, that there exists a
maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$ containing $\mathfrak{C}_\theta+p\mathcal{O}_K$, and let
$F=\mathcal{O}_K/\mathfrak{m}$. As above,
$\bar f(\bar\theta)=\bar f'(\bar\theta)=0.
$
By Proposition~\ref{prop:residue}, $\bar\theta$ satisfies
\eqref{eq:lin}, and Proposition~\ref{prop:Dzero} therefore yields
$\bar D=0
\quad\text{in }F.$
By Lemma~\ref{lem:intmem}, this implies that $p\mid D$, contradicting
our assumption. Hence no such maximal ideal exists, and
$\mathbb{Z}[\theta]$ is $p$-maximal. This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:master}
Let $f=X^n+a_{n-1}X^{n-1}+\dots+a_1X+a_0\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$ be monic and irreducible
with $n\ge2$, let $\theta$ be a root of $f$, and let $p$ be a prime.  If
$p\mid a_1$ and $p^2\mid a_0$, then $f$ is
non-monogenic.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Note that $p\mid I(\theta)$ by  Theorem~\ref{thm:nec} as $f(0)=a_0$ and $f'(0)=a_1$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:wild}
Let $f=X^n+a_{n-1}X^{n-1}+\dots+a_0\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$ be monic and irreducible with
root $\theta$, and let $p$ be a prime such that $p\mid n,~\text{and}~ p\mid a_i \text{ whenever } p\nmid i. $ If $p^2\mid f(r)$ for a single $r\in\mathbb{Z}$, then $p\mid I(\theta)$; in particular
$f$ is not monogenic.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
By given hypothesis, every coefficient of
$f'=\sum_i i\,a_iX^{i-1}$ is divisible by $p$, that is $\bar f'=0$.  Hence
$p\mid f'(r)$ for every $r\in\mathbb{Z}$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:nec} applies.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:fam1}
Let $p\ne q$ be primes, $k\in\mathbb{Z}$, $n>m\geq 2$, and  let
$f(X)=X^n+qk\,X^m+p^2q$.
Then $f$
is non-monogenic.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Note that $f$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$ and $p\mid I(\theta)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:nec}.  Hence $f$ is non-monogenic.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
Consider $f(X)=X^{35}+2X^2+18.
$ Here $p=3$, $q=2$, $k=1$, $n=35$, and $m=2.$ Hence  $f$ is non-monogenic by above Proposition.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
Let
$f(X)=X^{16}+10X^3+20.
$ Here $p=2$, $q=5$, $k=2$, $n=16$, and $m=3$. Hence $f$ is non-monogenic.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:translate}
Applying Corollary~\ref{cor:master} to $f(X+r)$, whose constant and linear
coefficients are $f(r)$ and $f'(r)$, returns Theorem~\ref{thm:nec} at a
general $r$; conversely, every application of Theorem~\ref{thm:nec} is an
application of Corollary~\ref{cor:master} to a translate of $f$.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:quadrinomial}
Let $n\ge3$ and $a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}$ with $b^2=ac$, and let
$f(X)=X^n+aX^2+2bX+c$ be irreducible with root $\theta$.  If $p$ is a prime
with $p\mid c$ and $p\nmid a$, then $p\mid I(\theta)$; in particular $f$ is
non-monogenic.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Proof is an immediate consequence of Corollary~\ref{cor:master}.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{ex:quadrinomial}
Let $f(X)=X^5+X^2+6X+9$.  Taking $p=3$, Proposition~\ref{prop:quadrinomial}
gives $3\mid I(\theta)$ and hence $f$ is non-monogenic.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
Recall that for $c\in\mathbb{Z}$ the residue $c^{\,p}\bmod p^2$ depends only on $c$ modulo $p$,
since $(c+p)^p\equiv c^{\,p}\pmod {p^2}$.  Write
$\omega(c)\in\mathbb{Z}/p^2\mathbb{Z}$ for this residue; the $p$ values
$\omega(0),\dots,\omega(p-1)$ are the Teichm\"uller lifts of $\mathbb{F}_p$.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:powcomp}
Let $p$ be a prime, let $g\in\mathbb{Z}[X]$ be monic, and let $f(X)=g(X^p)$ be
irreducible with root $\theta$.  If
\[
g\bigl(\omega(c)\bigr)\equiv0 \pmod{p^2}\qquad\text{for some }c\in\{0,\dots,p-1\},
\]
then $p\mid I(\theta)$; in particular $f$ is not monogenic.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Note that $f'(X)=p\,X^{p-1}g'(X^p)$, and
$f(c)=g(c^{\,p})\equiv g(\omega(c))\equiv0 \pmod{p^2}$.  Thus, $f$ is non-monogenic by Lemma~\ref{lem:wild} with $r=c$.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
\label{ex:powcomp}
Let $p=3$, so $\omega(0)=0$, $\omega(1)=1$, $\omega(2)=8$. Then
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] $g=Y^2+5Y+3$ has $g(1)=9$, so  
$3\mid I(\theta)$ and $X^6+5X^3+3$ is non-monogenic.
\item[(ii)] $g=Y^2-7Y+1$ has $g(8)=9$, so $X^6-7X^3+1$ is non-monogenic.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end example-4 -->
